content.thinking:
Bash is working now, though I noticed an odd message about renders being unavailable, possibly a leftover tool hook from an earlier command. I'll move forward with typecheck and preview to confirm things work properly.

Now I'm designing the character model in detail, settling on orientation conventions (left side in world space is +X) and planning the asymmetry — a mechanical left arm versus a staff-wielding right hand. For the palette, I'm going with an Overwatch-style clean look: white and navy armor with steel accents, using paint-based countershading for subtle depth rather than a toon-style outline kit.

I'm narrowing the accent colors down to a single strong green, dropping extra gold/amber ideas to keep it minimal, and settling on skin tones, a dark navy-black hair color tied in a high ponytail with a green hair tie for contrast against the white armor.

I'm now sketching the skeleton hierarchy, starting from the hip root and working out leg joint positions...

Still mapping leg joint chains...

Now I'm thinking through the leg radii tapering and armor details—thigh plating, knee guards, shin greaves with glowing strips, and chunky boots with sole stripes—plus considering giving the left arm a fully robotic, cybernetic look.

I'm also planning the torso: a pelvic armor belt with pouches and a holster, a glowing power-core on the chest, and a backpack healing emitter. For symbols, I'm avoiding any logo-like medic cross and instead leaning toward a stylized hexagon core light with maybe a subtle generic plus on the med pouch.

Now I'm figuring out the undersuit loft stations running up the spine, narrowing at the waist and widening at the chest/shoulders before tapering into the neck, with the loft's width and depth tied to the sideways and front-back dimensions along the path. I'm setting the loft's bone chain to run from the hips joint up through the spine so the sweep follows the skeleton correctly, starting at the pelvis height.

To keep things manageable I'm deciding to rig most armor pieces as rigid parts and reserve smooth/loft deformation only for limbs and the torso, then moving on to placing the shoulder and clavicle joints for the arms.

Setting up the arm chain with an A-pose angle, calculating shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand-tip positions using the hang angle and segment lengths...

For the right arm holding the staff, I need an asymmetric pose where the elbow bends forward and the hand grips the staff around waist height, differing from the resting left arm.

Placing the hand at the staff with fingers curling around it as wrapping arcs, with the thumb positioned opposite to complete the grip.

Setting wrist and hand tip joints to continue the forearm direction, then planning finger chains: three joints per finger times four fingers plus a two-joint thumb per hand, keeping the left hand relaxed and open while the cyborg hand uses segmented robotic fingers. I'm tallying the full joint budget across hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, clavicles, arms, and fingers to stay well under the 160 limit.

Legs, ponytail, staff, and backpack add roughly to a total near 60 joints, which is comfortable. Now I'm working out how to position the finger roots relative to each hand's local coordinate frame, using directional offsets like right/left/up/down/forward/back to place them naturally along the hanging arm.

Writing finger geometry logic...

Computing finger positions as points around the staff's circumference, spaced along its axis, sweeping from the medial/palm side toward the front using a circular parametrization around the staff's center.

I'm trying to work out the geometry of a right hand gripping a vertical staff in a fist shape, figuring out where the palm, wrapped fingers, and thumb should sit angularly around the staff so the pose looks anatomically correct.

I'm checking the wrist and forearm placement against the elbow, finding the distance too short at 0.17 when it needs to be 0.27, so I need to reposition the elbow higher to get the upper arm length right.

Trying upper arm 0.30, forearm 0.26 from shoulder to wrist: the straight-line distance is only 0.45 while the combined arm length is 0.56, so the elbow needs noticeable bend. I'm setting up a bend direction pointing back and down to get a realistic ~90-degree elbow angle.

I'm also checking the left arm span against its segment lengths, confirming a similar slight bend works, then naming the three-point chains for both arms so I can connect shoulder, elbow, and wrist consistently.

Adding a fourth joint for the hand tip at the end of the wrist, then deciding that finger chains should parent off the wrist joint so the palm moves naturally with it.

I'll compute the hand joint by extending the wrist position along the elbow-to-wrist direction, using Vector3 math from THREE. For the right arm this keeps the hand angled consistently with the forearm for gripping the staff, while the left hand stays open and relaxed with fingers extended.

Planning the two arms now: the right arm gets a navy suit sleeve with white armor pieces (pauldron, elbow pad, vambrace with green stripe) and a gloved hand, while the left arm is fully cybernetic with gunmetal segmented rings glowing green, hydraulic pistons in the forearm, and a mechanical hand with jointed steel fingers. I'm sketching out helper functions like a box-geometry builder to construct these pieces efficiently per body region.

Now I'm working through the extrusion logic for beveled armor panels, figuring out axis orientation so front-facing plates extrude correctly in the Z direction, then laying out the chest plate's front-view outline as a tapered polygon from wide shoulders down to a V-neck waist.

I'll default the undersuit loft to circular sections but size the chest plates to sink slightly into the surface, with a 0.05 thickness so the plate sits proud at center but recedes a bit at the edges to follow the torso curvature.

I'm structuring the build with small helper functions for parts and planning the paint scheme: countershaded white on top fading to light grey-blue underneath, plus panel lines and SVG decals for the chest core pattern.

Now I'm breaking down the full model into components, starting with the head: a skull sphere scaled to roughly match human head proportions, positioned at the head bone, with skin tones using the countershade helper.

For the jaw, I'm giving it its own bone with a joint that aims forward-down, using a scaled sphere for the lower jaw shape to form the chin. I'm making sure the face decal lands correctly by placing the mouth decal on the skull's lower portion rather than the jaw bone, and adjusting the skull sphere's size and position so there's enough chin area for the face to read properly.

I'm designing the face SVG with stylized almond eyes, lashes, brows, and lips, sized to fit the head front. For the left side, I'm planning a cybernetic cheek plate with a glowing green optic lens replacing that eye, built as a separate 3D piece with a ring and glow effect rather than drawn in the texture.

Now I'm thinking about the hair: a dark hair cap using a partial sphere scaled and shifted to cover the top and back of the skull, with an undercut effect on one side.

For the hairline, I'm planning to tilt the sphere cap backward by rotating around the X axis so the covered region leans away from the face, plus adding swoop bangs and a high ponytail chain with four joints and a tie.

Testing more elevation angles with the tilted-cap geometry confirms coverage down to about 20-40° at the forehead and down to roughly -35° at the nape, matching a natural hairline. I'm now settling on the scale factor for the cap to fit this coverage.

For the hair, I'm planning a high ponytail from the back-top, defined as a chain of joints following a catmull-rom path that curves down and inward, with the sweep radius bulging and tapering toward the tip, ending near the shoulder blades while staying clear of the backpack.

For the cyber face, I'm sketching a left cheek plate as an extruded steel-colored outline over the cheek and eye socket area.

I'm working out exact placement math for a gunmetal eye-socket plate on the skull's ellipsoid surface, solving for the z-coordinate so it sits flush against the curved face, then considering using a decal approach with an SVG texture showing a cyborg eye plate with a green glowing iris ring and scan lines, possibly layered with a separate glow element.

Now I'm planning additional cyber details: a cheekbone armor plate over the left temple, an ear piece with a lathed steel disc and green ring, a small antenna, and a skin sphere for the right ear. I'm also sketching the neck construction with a navy undersuit sweep, a collar ring, and gunmetal cable lines, then moving into torso design with a navy undersuit and a white V-shaped chest plate featuring a glowing hexagonal core.

For the back I'm designing a boxy medical-style backpack unit with a gunmetal frame, twin glowing green canister tubes in clear cradles, top intake vents, lower exhaust cones, and a central glow strip, sizing it roughly as a rounded box positioned behind the torso.

Instead of Mercy-style wings I want two angled stabilizer fins at the pack's top, white with green edge glow, giving a distinctive silhouette without copying existing designs. For the waist, I'm planning a gunmetal belt loop with a buckle plate, front tasset and side hip armor plates, skipping a cape, plus a pair of medical pouches with plus decals and a small vial rack on the hip.

For the legs, navy thigh sweeps with white front armor plates, green-inlaid knee pads, white shin guards with a green stripe, and heavy boots built from a lathed ankle cuff, foot box, toe cap, sole slab, and heel block. I'll make the left leg partially cyber, exposing gunmetal pistons and ring joints beneath a cutaway calf casing.

For the staff in the right hand, I'm sizing it around 1.55m with a two-tone gunmetal/white shaft, navy grip wraps near the hand, and glowing green rings along its length.

Now I'm designing the staff head: a crescent cradle of curved prongs holding a glowing green orb with an orbit ring, plus a hex-pattern decal and energy gauge on the shaft, deciding the staff should top out around 1.9m to extend slightly above the character's 1.82m height, and setting up the joint attachment at the shaft's base relative to the hand.

I'm planning the decal layers for facial and surface detail — eye with lashes, brow and nose/mouth shading, a cybernetic eye plate with scan rings on the left side, and considering a 3D glyph for the chest core — along with making sure both the staff base and boots sit flush on the floor.

I'm expanding the decal set further: hex/carbon plating for the cyber arm and backpack vents, a green medical cross on pouches, hazard stripe labels like unit codes on the shoulder and staff rendered as SVG text, rune-style gauge markings along the staff shaft, and painted hair grain with highlights. For the armor paint, I'm combining a subtle countershade with mottled panel dirt to give the white base form and wear.

I'm now defining color treatments for each material: countershaded mottle for armor, navy and gunmetal suits, brushed steel grain, warm skin tones, and an emissive green glow for highlighted elements. I'm also setting budget targets around 500 parts and under 60k triangles, then moving into writing the actual part placement code with bone attachments and rotations.

For geometry, I'm working out orientation rules for different primitive types—rods and frustum boxes default to specific axis conventions, so I'm planning to use point-based primitives like sweeps and frustum boxes between joint locations to avoid manual rotation math, with rigid bone attachment for armor plates on limbs.

Now I'm sketching the actual implementation: setting up imports for the builder, path utilities, IK limb helper, and paint/texture modules, defining the metadata block, and building out a countershaded armor color palette with mottled texture variation.

Defining more color palette values...

I'm keeping the flat color count low while baking paints into one sheet, then starting the skeleton builder with hip and spine joints using catmull-rom chains.

Continuing with neck and head joints, chaining parents from the spine's last joint and setting head orientation and direction values.

Adding joint definitions for the jaw and clavicles...

I'm defining the arm chain as a sequence of joints from shoulder through elbow and wrist, with the whole chain tagged with the arm role and parented at the chest spine joint, then setting up a sweep along that path for the limb skin geometry.

I'll use a catmull spline through shoulder, elbow, and wrist for a smooth organic bone-skinned sweep, accepting that it deviates slightly from the exact joint corners. Now I'm tapering the radii along the arm — upper arm from about 0.052 at the shoulder down to 0.045 at the elbow, then forearm from 0.045 down to 0.034 toward the wrist.

For the legs, I'm setting up a loop over left/right sides that computes hip and ankle target positions, runs them through the limb solver with upper/lower leg lengths of 0.44 and 0.42 to get hip, knee, and ankle points, then builds a chain with those as named joints — giving the chain a tip joint at the ankle, parented to the hip.

I'm adding the toe joint parented to the ankle, positioned and aimed forward as a hinge, and checking that the boot/sole geometry sits correctly relative to ankle height. Then I'm checking hip and thigh widths against the torso width to make sure the legs don't clip through the hips.

Now I'm lofting the torso through six stations from hip to chest, giving it a waist taper and chest bulge, bound to the hip and spine bones with a navy color. I'm noting that the spine bone chain uses a slightly different catmull curve than the torso loft silhouette, so I need to be careful the skin weights project correctly onto the actual bone path.

Checking shoulder joint placement so the arm socket radius lines up smoothly with the chest plate width at the top of the torso, aiming for an androgynous athletic build. Now I'm sketching the chest armor plate outline as a set of 2D points around the chest center, shaping a V-neck silhouette before extruding it into a plate.

I'm placing the plate center at z=0.105 with thickness 0.045, but noticing the plate's wide edges at ±0.185 extend beyond the torso's actual half-width of about 0.17 at that height, meaning the plate overhangs the torso surface there.

Checking the gap more carefully, narrowing the plate's half-width to 0.15 still leaves about a 1.5cm floating gap between the plate's inner surface and the torso's ellipse surface — not ideal, so I need to tighten this further.

Raising the plate's center z to .095 with .07 thickness gives a front face at .13 (slightly proud of torso front at .122) and a back face at .06 that tucks inside the torso surface at the edges — that fixes the sinking issue at the plate's center, though .07 thickness feels heavy and may need a bevel to soften.

Now I'm planning the remaining torso details: lower abdomen plates, a hexagonal sternum core with a glowing inner disc, a collar ring around the neck base, a thinner mirrored back plate for pack mounting, and the backpack's main body built from tapered box frustums.

For the backpack I'm adding glowing vertical canisters on each side with gunmetal brackets, plus intake boxes with grille details and side fin extrusions. Then I'm shifting focus to the overall "Overwatch" aesthetic -- large bevelled panels accented with thin dark seam lines, implemented as slender rods laid along surfaces like the chest plate.

I'm reconsidering that approach though, since many thin rods would be tedious -- instead I'll use a flat SVG decal plane positioned just above the chest plate's front face, drawing panel seams and rivets as dark lines on a transparent background so the plate color shows through everywhere else. I'm mapping out the texture coordinates to match the plate's physical dimensions before sketching the line layout.

Now I'm planning the seam and rivet positions for the SVG, converting between world coordinates and texture pixel space, and setting up the plane geometry to sit flush against the plate's front surface. Next I'll move on to building the shoulder pauldrons as large rounded lathe-shaped armor pieces.

Closing the lathe profile back to the axis and adding a thin flat green accent ring at the rim for the trim detail, keeping it non-glowing for contrast with the armor.

Now I'm defining two distinct green tones: a flat accent trim color and a brighter emissive glow color for the lit segments. The pauldron mounts rigidly on the shoulder bone joint, which works well.

For the left cyborg arm, I'm planning exposed mechanical detailing on the upper arm—a gunmetal rod core with short steel ring segments and thin glowing green ring accents along its length.

I'm continuing into the piston, ball-joint elbow, armored forearm sleeve with glowing vein lines, and a mechanical glove hand built from boxes and small sphere joints for fingers. The right arm gets contrasting organic armor treatment—navy sleeves, white vambrace, and a gloved hand with a white knuckle plate. I'm planning to write a reusable `buildArm` function that takes computed limb points and constructs each arm's geometry from shared helper logic.

Writing finger generation function...

For fingertips I'll just add small box caps rather than organic nails. Four fingers plus a thumb across three joints each gives fifteen joints per hand, thirty total; I'm now working out the thumb's two-span structure and positioning the left hand's palm and finger roots relative to the hand direction and lateral offset vector.

Since the left hand's palm faces medially toward the body rather than down, I realize the fingers need to line up front-to-back along the z-axis instead of side-to-side along x, with the thumb set slightly forward of the other fingers.

Computing finger rotation axes and spread angles...

Calculating the right hand's grip geometry around the staff, placing finger root points on a wrapping circle offset by the staff radius plus finger thickness, starting from an angle offset of -75°.

Still positioning the palm box...

For the fist, I need the fingers to wrap from the palm around the staff, so I'm setting finger root positions along the palm edge closest to the staff axis.

Since the finger roots line up vertically along the staff while the forearm runs diagonally, I should orient the palm block vertically instead, covering the staff's y-range behind the fingers, centered around (-0.49, 1.0, 0.12) with a thin vertical profile.

I'm sizing the palm box so its front surface roughly touches the staff's back surface, then planning a thumb wrap on the opposite side and working out where the fingertips end relative to the wrist and thumb root angles.

Now I'm setting the thumb's path over the top of the fingers at a different angle than the fingers themselves, skipping full anatomical realism, and deciding the staff should be rigidly attached to its own wrist joint rather than independently animated.

Working out the staff's dimensions now: a lower shaft section in steel, then a tapered rubber ferrule tip at the bottom of the rod, building up the overall height toward the orb section.

Continuing the geometry, I'm adding collar rings, a navy grip with spiral stripes, a white upper shaft with glowing green inlay segments, and a wider lathe collar base before reaching the head.

For the head itself, I'm shaping a glowing orb centered higher up, surrounded by three curved prongs sweeping outward from the collar and bulging around the orb before tapering to tips, plus a thin tilted torus ring orbiting the sphere for extra detail.

I'll skip the holo plus shape and extra floating details, instead focusing on the cyborg's left eye with a glowing lens and angled cheek plate. For the face decals, I'm sketching the right eye as an SVG with an almond-shaped sclera, gradient iris, pupil, highlight, and lash lines.

Still writing SVG eye details...

Decal targets both skull and jaw parts so the mouth spans the seam correctly. For the eyes, I'm positioning projection decals near the face front at the correct offsets, and designing the cyber eye with a dark socket, green iris ring, scanning crosshair, and small LED details, plus a glowing lens sphere for depth.

Wrapping the decal in glow() should light up the bright texture areas while leaving dark parts unaffected. Now I'm working out the side cheek plate geometry — figuring out the local coordinate axes so the plate's thickness runs correctly along the head's width, then sketching the outline in side profile to cover the temple and cheek area near the ear.

Checking the plate against the skull surface equation at different z-heights shows it floats off the head past a certain point, so a flat extruded plate won't conform properly. I'm considering switching to a sweep or drape-based approach that follows the skull's curvature instead, maybe using a swept rim outline rather than a rigid flat shape.

Actually, projecting a flat decal onto the surface seems cleaner for the cyber plate look — I can paint an angular panel shape with seam glow lines directly onto the geometry rather than trying to extrude solid plates. I'll use a front-facing decal for the eye and cheek region, plus a second side-facing decal for the temple area, so each projection stays roughly perpendicular to the surface it's covering and avoids stretching.

I need to keep the glowing eye ring as a separate decal from the plain plate panel so the glow doesn't bleed into the metal, aligning both decals' dimensions and direction so they register correctly, with the glow layer lifted slightly higher off the surface. Then I'm placing hair to cover the forehead above the hairline, positioning the right ear as a simple skin sphere and the left ear as a cybernetic piece with a steel disc, green ring, and antenna rod, and finally sweeping the neck geometry from chest to jaw with a tapering radius along a curved centerline.

Now I'm working out the collar and boot details: a lathed navy ring for the undersuit collar plus a white gorget plate pair, a simple pelvis block for the hip underside, and defining helper functions like a vector constructor to keep the code clean. For the boots, I'm sweeping tapered box shapes from ankle to shin for the shaft, keeping the toe cap on its own bone, and coloring everything dark navy-gray with a white toe accent.

Adding velcro strap boxes across the instep, then setting toe joint positions and assigning the sole slab to the ankle bone. Now I'm planning the leg bones per side, starting with a navy thigh sweep following a curve from hip through knee.

For the left leg's cyborg shin, I need the color to switch to gunmetal below the knee, but the color parameter needs to be a string or function returning a string, so I'm working out how to express that band transition.

Now I'm figuring out the thigh armor plate placement, positioning a frustum box along the thigh that sits flush against the front surface without clipping into the leg geometry.

For the knee pad, I'm planning a shield-shaped extrusion positioned at the knee joint, with a thin green inlay accent layered on top as a smaller, slightly extruded detail piece.

For the shin, I'm shaping a tapered frustum guard with a white body and green stripe decal, plus a thin glow rod running down the front centerline. I'm making the left leg distinctly cybernetic—exposed piston hydraulics and a steel rod/sleeve at the calf replacing the organic armor guard, while the right leg stays armored and organic for contrast.

Now I'm working on the pelvis belt: I'm sweeping a closed loop path around the waist using the torso surface, trying to figure out the right section radius orientation for a wide band shape. The binormal direction for a horizontal loop is ambiguous, so I'm testing a box cross-section and will verify the look visually before committing to specific width/height values.

Considering alternatives like lathing a belt ring, but the torso is elliptical rather than circular so a lathe wouldn't match the shape without scaling, and I'm unsure how to apply non-uniform scale to a lathed part. Sticking with the surface loop approach since it naturally conforms to the torso's actual contour, then moving on to designing trapezoidal hip tassets extruded at an angle on each side.

Working out box dimensions for the hip plates so they sit just outside the thigh sweep radius for floating armor coverage, then adding angular side fins, a small rear back panel under the pack, and a pair of pouches on the right hip with lids.

On the left hip I'm adding a vial rack of three glowing capsule cylinders mounted in a gunmetal holder, plus a few thin cable sweeps running from the backpack side around the rear shoulder to the upper arm, rigged to the chest bone so they stay plausible across the joint. That's enough detailing -- time to actually write the file.

Given its length, I'm planning helper functions for box, sphere, and cylinder geometry, a generic part-placement helper that takes geometry, color, bone, position, and optional scale, and a loop pattern for mirroring left/right side parts. I'm also setting up SVG texture generators for panel details like the chest plate, starting with the chest texture first.

Writing SVG seam lines...

Adding label text and green accent lines...

Now I'm computing where the plate plane should sit relative to the core housing, mirroring positions behind the hex core to avoid visual overlap, and working out the plate's center coordinates and z-depth offset for the front-facing decal.

Next I'm sketching the pouch icon as a simple rounded square outline with a plus symbol inside, then noting I still need the face SVGs and cyber-themed elements.

For the forearm, I'm planning a decal technique using hex-grid texture patterns to add vents and panel lines onto the plating, and I'm setting up a similar decal approach for a tall gauge strip with tick marks onto the staff's shaft.

Now I'm thinking through the backpack grille slots as a decal on the back flat face, plus adding a small "07" text label decal on the shoulder pauldron or possibly the pack/hip instead. I also need to remember the ponytail hair piece should chain-parent to the head, and I should be careful about unused imports and variables causing typecheck errors once I start writing the actual code.

Writing skeleton and arm chain code...

I'm deciding to use a simple polyline through shoulder, elbow, and wrist for the sweep path, letting it end at the wrist with a round cap, and computing radii along the path by arc-length parameterization.

Now I'm moving on to finger placement, planning distinct designs for the open left hand versus gripping right hand on the cyber arm, and writing a helper function that builds finger joint points by curling along a rotation axis derived from the base direction and curl direction vectors.

Still working out hand geometry...

Working out the thumb geometry now—placing its root offset from the wrist using the front and curl directions, then rotating the thumb's base direction toward the front by roughly 38° using a cross-product axis derived from the direction and front vectors. I'll define a general "toward" helper function that rotates a direction vector toward a target by some angle, and apply it here rather than hardcoding each case.

Now I'm sketching out the hand geometry itself: approximating the palm as a thin box (with local axes set so the direction vector is the length axis), sized roughly 0.075 wide, 0.09 long, 0.032 thick, usable for both hands. For the cyber hand variant, I'm planning a gun-metal palm with a steel back plate and a glowing green dot, finger sections as small boxes, and tiny spheres at the knuckle joints. I'm about to write out the full implementation code.

Computing finger joint positions around the staff...

For the thumb, I'll position its root near the medial-back side and angle it to cross over the fingers at the top, mimicking how a thumb wraps over a fist. I'm giving the hand a navy glove color with a lighter knuckle plate detail, keeping fingertip rendering simple.

Now I'm moving to the right arm's armor pieces: a pauldron at the shoulder, a navy upper-arm sleeve, a white bicep band, an elbow pad, and a tapered forearm vambrace built as a sweeping box shape along the elbow-to-wrist bone, sized to taper from wider near the elbow to narrower at the wrist, all in white with a possible thin accent stripe.

Rather than figuring out exact surface orientation for a stripe, I'm simplifying by using small accent rings around the forearm axis instead, since that's orientation-independent. Then I move to the left cyborg arm, starting with a gun-barrel-like upper arm sweep and steel rings around it.

For the elbow I'm placing a sphere joint with two gunmetal side discs, and for the forearm a tapered core with armor strips arranged around the axis using perpendicular vectors computed from the arm direction, so I build a generic helper to place plates evenly around any axis.

I'll define a plate helper function for armor pieces, then build the left forearm as a smooth skinned sweep with rigid armor plates layered on top. After the arm and hand parts, I'm thinking through the overall silhouette: broad shoulders and chest, tapered waist, stylized boots, and ponytail details to give that Overwatch-style look.

For the hair, I'm sculpting a cap base with extruded bangs sweeping across the forehead and a ponytail made of tapered strand sweeps tied off at the back, calculating the geometry so the bangs curve naturally along the skull's surface at the hairline.

Anchoring bangs...

Confirming -31.5° tilt points the pole backward correctly, and the cap being slightly oversized should compensate for the rotation mismatch with the skull mesh. Now I'm starting to write out the full file with scoped helper functions for vectors.

Defining color palette and skeleton joints...

Adding more body parts now—pelvis block, arms, legs, and a pauldron shoulder piece built with a lathe profile, making sure the outline curve closes cleanly back to the axis.

Still shaping lathe outlines...

I also need a thin neck cable sweep and left ear piece, then move to the staff hand position checks before writing it all out and running the typecheck/preview pass.

Checking the arm reach: with shoulder at (-0.205,1.42,0) and wrist at the chosen grip point, the distance comes out to about 0.455, comfortably within the 0.56 limb limit, so the pose should work once the elbow bend is applied.

Now I'm working out the ponytail chain, laying out points from the back of the head down to a curved tail tip across four named segments.

I need to shorten the path so it clears the backpack top -- adjusting the tail endpoint upward and tweaking the z-depth to keep it from clipping the pack. I'm also setting up the radius taper for each ponytail segment and planning a small lathe ring accent at the base to act as a hair tie, then moving on to write the file.

Now I'm working out the limb and loop helper calls -- checking joint positions along the spine so I can place a belt loop at waist height (y=1.0) using the torso's horizontal cross-section, making sure the loop correctly wraps around the point where the legs and torso meet.

input.command: cat package.json | head -30; sed -n 1,60p src/frame.ts | head -80; grep -n "export" src/index.ts | head
